claims.text: The experimental baseline is undoped Al0.1CoCrFeNi high-entropy nanoalloy.
Al0.1CoCrFeNi high-entropy nanoalloys can be prepared by established methods.
A low weight percentage of Sc will be introduced into Al0.1CoCrFeNi.
Sc addition modifies the local mixing enthalpy of Al0.1CoCrFeNi.
Sc addition reduces atomic misfit in Al0.1CoCrFeNi.
The proposed changes in mixing enthalpy and atomic misfit energetically retard atomic segregation.
Retarded segregation suppresses thermally activated chemical clustering.
Retarded segregation suppresses secondary-phase formation and phase separation.
Sc addition can produce grain-boundary precipitates in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
Sc addition changes lattice parameters in the target nanoalloy.
Sc addition enhances high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
Sc-doped material will exhibit delayed high-temperature phase evolution relative to the undoped baseline.
Sc-doped material will exhibit a reduced extent or lower rate of secondary-phase formation relative to the undoped baseline.
Sc-doped material will exhibit less chemical clustering than the undoped baseline.
Sc doping will maintain a more homogeneous disordered phase during high-temperature cycling.
The prediction applies up to approximately 1000 K in controlled atmospheres.
Significantly higher Sc content may produce additional phases or unexpected interactions.
The stabilizing effect may be subtle and influenced by concurrent high-temperature processes.
In situ high-temperature XRD can monitor phase appearance and lattice-parameter evolution during the comparison.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant delay or reduction in secondary-phase formation and chemical clustering in the Sc-doped samples is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Grain-boundary precipitate formation is named as a mediator, while the proposed mechanism and prediction broadly describe suppression of segregation and secondary-phase formation. The hypothesis does not distinguish stabilizing Sc-rich precipitates from the secondary phases it predicts will be reduced.
